plunge_ramp.applies: stated for down-cut and compression tools; used for all tool types as the conservative default

lead_in_out.note: No vendor publishes a separate lead-in feed. An arc lead-in enters at reduced radial engagement, so the cutting feed is safe there.

chip_floor_mm_per_tooth.note: a minimum, not a target - the only limit that increases the feed; marginal_below is the close-to-minimum band boundary from the reference status chips

depth_limit.note: the vendor depth rule (Onsrud, Amana, Freud) ends at its 3xD anchor and no chart publishes deeper. Until 2026-08-29 a hyperbolic extension (0.5 x 3/ratio) served past it, which shrank the chip until the floor warning fired against the served number and told the user to raise a feed the calculator had just lowered. A review sweep found 1,260 such results per profile. The calculator now blocks past 3xD and names the maximum pass (Scott, 2026-08-29). Amendment 2026-09-02 (Scott): the block covers slot-width cuts only. The depth hazard is engagement, not flute immersion. A cut under half the diameter wide clears its chips sideways and runs the flute length at a light optimal load as standard adaptive practice, so light-radial cuts lose the depth derate and the block; chip thinning already compensates their programmed feed. A pass deeper than a known flute length draws a hot warning (past_flutes), never a block.
depth_limit.applies_to: slot-width cuts only: width of cut at or above half the tool diameter

compression_min_depth.note: Vortex: a 0.5 in up-cut length must cut a minimum of 0.563 in per pass; up-cut length is usually about 1xD

corner_model.form: L = v^2/a (decelerate into the corner plus accelerate out, each v^2/2a)

profile_bands.note: gentle/standard/aggressive = lower edge/midpoint/upper edge of the SERVED band (decision D11, 2026-08-18): the geometry-and-diameter-matched charts when they exist, otherwise the generic charts; other vendors render as named context

finishing.note: the Finishing profile serves the finisher-series charts (Onsrud 60-200), the only published finishing chip loads, at their low edge, as the PROGRAMMED chip with no chip-thinning compensation, because the vendor publishes them for a finish pass with its light radial engagement already inside the number. Panels with no finisher chart (plywood, soft plywood, melamine, HPL) borrow the MDF finisher chart, the lowest of the three, with a note. Outside the finisher rows' diameter coverage the profile refuses. The deep-slot depth derate does not apply to a skim (under half the diameter wide). When no width of cut is given it assumes 1 mm of radial stock on the wall. All of these are Scott's calls (2026-08-29): the skim sits inside Leitz's published 1-2 mm finish allowance, and the programmed-chip serve replaced two earlier builds the same day, one serving the tool chart's own low edge (24,300 mm/min on an MDF half-inch skim) and one compensating the finisher chip for thinning (30,000 mm/min on a 3/4 in three-flute hardwood skim), both rejected as numbers no machinist would run. The first-cut reduction never applies in this profile: it compensates heavy engagement, and on a thin skim a reduced feed drives the chip under the rubbing floor.

first_cut.note: the first cut runs at 65% of the served chart feed; work up toward the chart value once the cut proves out (decision D15; the README has promised conservative dial-in from the start)

big_iron_caveat.applies_when: every chart setting the served band carries machine_class big_iron_10hp_plus
big_iron_caveat.message: These values come only from charts written for rigid industrial machines with 10+ hp spindles. No conservative source (Onsrud, ITA) publishes this material, so there is nothing here to temper them. Treat the Gentle end as the starting point and prove it with a test cut.

envelope_rules.note: a diameter-resolved chart contributes only within +/-25% of its published diameter range; when the charts eligible to set a band disagree by more than 2x in midpoint, the most conservative chart serves and the rest become context (decision D11)

drilling.note: the published speed range is the served value (decision 2, 2026-09-01): surface speed and feed per revolution are derived display and no speed is ever back-derived from a surface speed. standard_band_position is 0.5, the midpoint, so the profile words mean the same thing as in routing (Scott, 2026-09-02, decision 8). diameter_coverage_tolerance is 0, not the routing 0.25, because a drill's diameter range is a range of tools with nothing to interpolate between: +/-25% on a 15-40 mm hinge drill would serve 11 mm and 50 mm cutters that do not exist. Outside the published speed range the feed per revolution holds flat at the nearest edge and a warning says so, which is conservative because the band's upper edge falls as speed rises. first_cut_applies is false (Scott, 2026-09-02, decision 10): the band's lower edge is already the rubbing floor, and 65% of a published plunge feed drives the cut under it, which in a blind hole burns. missing_material_factor serves the lowest published factor in the tool's own table when the table has no row for the picked material (Scott, 2026-09-02, decision 9), with a rendered note. band_ratio_sanity is a read gate, not a served value. Measured across the 17 accepted diagrams the bands run 1.64x to 4.94x, widest at the slow end of each range and narrowing as speed rises, so the bound is set from that spread with headroom. It still catches the read that goes badly wrong, which is taking the whole plot rectangle for the band and gives a far larger number. The research's earlier 'about 2:1' came from the hinge-drill diagram alone and does not hold across the chapter. band_coverage_min is the second read gate: a diagram's band must cover at least this much of its tool's published speed range. Not all of it, because the source itself does not always draw all of it. The solid-carbide through-hole drill is rated to 12,000 rpm and its diagram stops near 9,000, and the hinge-drill polygons stop a whisker inside the axis end. Where the band stops the feed holds at that edge and the calculator says so, which is conservative because the upper edge falls as speed rises. A band covering less than this is reading the wrong diagram.

drill_peck_suggestion.note: most drills publish no chip-clearing rule at all, and saying nothing about a 5xD dowel hole is unhelpful when the chapter twice says what happens in a deep one (Scott, 2026-09-02). Past this depth the calculator suggests a clearing stroke on a drill whose own page publishes no rule, and labels the suggestion as borrowed rather than published. Two rules in the chapter carry it. The double-heel twist drill states a clearing stroke past 4xD, and the small boring pins make an interim chip-removal stroke obligatory in hardwood and glulam with a maximum infeed of 2xD, so the harder of the two published rules is stricter than the figure used here. It never overrides a tool's own published rule, and it deliberately does not touch the served feed: a suggestion may change what the user does, and only a published number may change what the calculator serves.

drilling_attribution.note: no vendor name renders anywhere in the drilling output (Scott, 2026-09-01, decision 7), a deliberate departure from routing, where the limit line and the chart ladder both name the serving chart. Provenance stays complete in data/drills.json, and only the rendering changes. The core enforces this by what it omits: a drilling result carries no contributors and no servingBands key, so the routing chart ladder cannot be pointed at one. Decision 4 (on irreconcilable disagreement the most conservative source serves alone) is recorded and dormant, because only one source serves drilling and nothing can yet disagree with it.

drill_bank.note: a drill bank is a fixed-speed geared head on the same machining centre, with its own drive. When the user says the drills run on a bank (a check box in the advanced panel, Scott's call 2026-09-02, decision 11), the router spindle's rated minimum speed no longer applies and the low-speed warning is suppressed, because the bank is not the spindle being warned about. No power figure is reported either: no source in session 5 publishes a drill-bank drive power, and reporting the router spindle's power for a cut the spindle is not making would be a number with nothing behind it. This replaced a drill-bank machine preset, which would have had to be appended rather than inserted, because the share link writes the machine preset as a positional index.
